column1: Themes were derived from the retained literature and used to connect evidence, contradictions, business decisions and artefact requirements. Study-specific results are compared rather than pooled into an assumed EcoLoop result.

column2: Hitt et al. (2023); Hoseini et al. (2024); Hitt et al. (2025)
column4: Reuse performance depends on completed cycles, washing, transport and scale.
column5: Published GWP break-even thresholds differ materially across system boundaries; values cannot be pooled.
column6: No generic carbon-saving claim; compare verified cycles and site conditions with named study thresholds.

column2: Greenwood et al. (2021); Collis et al. (2023); Hoseini et al. (2024)
column4: Participation and continued reuse depend on user acceptance as well as environmental design.
column5: Willingness, uptake, return and container condition are not equivalent; wear can reduce acceptance.
column6: Measure uptake and return separately; include inspection and retirement controls.

column4: Tracking can support asset, lifespan and cleaning evidence.
column5: Digital traceability cannot replace recovery, washing, food-safety control or reverse logistics.
column6: Use QR as a control layer within a return-wash-inspect-redistribute process.

column2: Ratay et al. (2024); Hitt et al. (2025)
column4: Dense networks can support acquisition and operating efficiency.
column5: Density does not guarantee repeat use; small centralised systems can underperform.
column6: Begin with a dense anchor-site pilot before geographic expansion.

column2: Bocken et al. (2022); Tenhunen-Lunkka et al. (2024)
column4: Participation, partners, operations, revenue and profitability are interdependent.
column5: Business-model frameworks identify conditions but do not prove EcoLoop site performance.
column6: Filter the Business Model Canvas through DFVS and require evidence gates before scale.
